title: Get Professional Help - Check, Call, Care
summary: Scene safety first, then call 911 for anything life-threatening.
quick_actions: Check: is the scene safe for YOU before approaching? Hazards can injure a second person trying to help.
Call 911 (or have someone else call) immediately if the person is unresponsive, not breathing or only gasping, has severe bleeding, or shows any obvious life-threatening condition.
Care: give the care you're trained and equipped for while help is on the way - don't attempt anything beyond that.
If multiple people are hurt, unresponsiveness and severe bleeding are the two conditions that need attention first.
more_info: This three-step framework (Check, Call, Care) is the foundation Red Cross first aid training is built on - apply it before any of the specific topics below.

title: CPR / AED Overview
summary: For an unresponsive person not breathing normally: call 911, get an AED, and begin CPR if trained.
quick_actions: Call 911 (or have someone call) and send someone to get an AED if one is available.
If trained: push hard and fast in the center of the chest, about 100-120 compressions per minute, allowing the chest to fully rise between compressions.
Use an AED as soon as one arrives - it will guide you with voice prompts; most models are designed for untrained bystanders to use.
Continue until EMS arrives, the person starts breathing normally, or an AED tells you to stop.
more_info: CPR quality (hand placement, depth, rate, rescue breaths) is a physical skill that genuinely requires hands-on practice - a free/low-cost Red Cross or AHA course teaches and lets you practice it properly. This overview is not a substitute for that training.
training_note: Hands-on certified training (Red Cross/AHA) is strongly recommended - this is a summary of what CPR/AED involves, not a substitute for practicing the technique.

title: Choking (Conscious Adult/Child)
summary: Alternate 5 back blows and 5 abdominal thrusts until the object clears.
quick_actions: Ask 'Are you choking?' - if they can cough, speak, or breathe, encourage coughing rather than intervening.
If they can't breathe/speak/cough: give 5 back blows between the shoulder blades, then 5 abdominal thrusts (pull inward and upward, above the navel).
Alternate 5-and-5 until the object comes out or the person can breathe, cough, or cry.
If the person becomes unresponsive: lower them to the ground and begin CPR, starting with compressions.
more_info: For someone too large to reach around, or who is pregnant, give chest thrusts instead of abdominal thrusts.

title: Severe (Life-Threatening) Bleeding
summary: Direct pressure first; a tourniquet if bleeding on a limb won't stop.
quick_actions: Call 911. Apply firm, direct pressure to the wound with a clean cloth, gauze, or your hand.
Keep pressing - don't peek or remove the material to check; add more on top if it soaks through.
If bleeding from an arm or leg won't stop with direct pressure and you have a tourniquet (and training), apply it 2-3 inches above the wound, tighten until bleeding stops.
Once a tourniquet is applied, do not loosen or remove it - that's for medical professionals only.
more_info: Severe blood loss can be fatal in minutes - don't wait to see if pressure alone is working before escalating to a tourniquet if one is available and the bleeding is on a limb.

title: Shock
summary: Pale, cool, clammy skin and a fast weak pulse are early warning signs.
quick_actions: Call 911 - shock is life-threatening and gets worse without treatment.
Have the person lie flat; if no sign of a broken bone or head/spine injury, raise their feet 6-12 inches.
Keep them warm and calm - anxiety and pain can make shock progress faster.
Don't give food or drink.
more_info: Shock commonly follows severe bleeding, serious injury, or a severe allergic reaction - treat it as an emergency even if the original cause seems to be improving.

title: Burns
summary: Cool the burn under clean, cool running water for 10-20 minutes.
quick_actions: Cool the burn under cool (not ice-cold) running water for at least 10-20 minutes - this both relieves pain and limits damage.
Remove tight items (rings, clothing) near the burn before swelling starts, if they aren't stuck to it.
Cover loosely with a clean, non-stick dressing - don't apply butter, oil, or ice.
Seek prompt medical care for large burns, burns with blisters covering a wide area, or burns on the face/hands/feet/genitals - and always for a child.
more_info: A burn that looks white, leathery, or charred, or any chemical/electrical burn, needs immediate emergency care - don't wait to see if it improves.

title: Minor Cuts & Wounds
summary: Clean it, cover it, and watch for signs of infection.
quick_actions: Wash your hands, then rinse the wound with clean water to remove dirt/debris.
Apply gentle direct pressure with clean gauze/cloth until any minor bleeding stops.
Apply a thin layer of antibiotic ointment (if no known allergy) and cover with a clean bandage.
Watch for infection over the following days: increasing redness, warmth, swelling, pus, red streaking, or fever - seek medical care if these appear.
more_info: Most small cuts and scrapes heal fine with basic cleaning and a clean dressing - this is for minor wounds only, not deep or heavily bleeding ones (see Severe Bleeding).

title: Sprains & Fractures
summary: Rest, immobilize, cool, and elevate - don't try to straighten a deformed limb.
quick_actions: Rest: stop using the injured area. Immobilize: keep it as still as possible, ideally splinted in the position found.
Cool: apply ice or a cold pack wrapped in cloth (never directly on skin) to reduce swelling.
Elevate the injured area above heart level if possible and if it doesn't cause more pain.
Seek medical care for a suspected fracture (deformity, inability to bear weight, bone visible through skin) - and call 911 for an open fracture or if it's a head/neck/back injury.
more_info: It's often not possible to tell a bad sprain from a fracture without an X-ray - when in doubt, treat it as a possible fracture and get it evaluated.

title: Head Injury Warning Signs
summary: Watch closely after any bump to the head - some warning signs appear later.
quick_actions: Call 911 immediately for: unresponsiveness, repeated vomiting, worsening/persistent headache, seizure, or a noticeable change in behavior or vision.
Any loss of consciousness, even brief, after a head injury deserves prompt medical evaluation.
Symptoms of a concussion can appear hours or even days after the injury - keep watching, don't assume you're clear just because nothing showed up right away.
Suspected neck/spine injury: keep the person as still as possible and avoid moving them unless there's immediate danger, until EMS arrives.
more_info: Most concussions don't need an ER visit, but any of the red-flag signs above do - when in doubt, get it checked.

title: Seizures
summary: Protect them from injury - don't restrain, and don't put anything in their mouth.
quick_actions: Help them to the ground, clear the area of anything they could hit, and cushion their head.
Do not restrain them and do not put anything in their mouth.
Time the seizure. Once it stops, roll them onto their side to help keep the airway clear.
Call 911 for: a first-time seizure, one lasting more than 5 minutes, repeated seizures without waking between, difficulty breathing afterward, or if it happened in water.
more_info: Stay with the person until they're fully alert - they may be confused or disoriented for a while after the seizure ends.

title: Poisoning
summary: Call Poison Control (1-800-222-1222) or 911 - don't guess at home remedies.
quick_actions: Call the National Poison Control Center: 1-800-222-1222 (free, 24/7, anywhere in the US) - or 911 if the person is unresponsive, having trouble breathing, or seizing.
Do not give anything to eat or drink, and do not try to induce vomiting, unless specifically told to by Poison Control or EMS.
If possible, have the container/substance on hand when you call - it helps them give the right instructions fast.
Follow their specific guidance exactly - poisoning first aid varies a lot by what was involved.
more_info: Poison Control is staffed by medical professionals and is almost always faster and safer than guessing - call before you act, not after.

title: Allergic Reaction / Anaphylaxis
summary: Anaphylaxis can turn life-threatening within minutes - epinephrine, not antihistamines, is the treatment.
quick_actions: Mild reaction (rash, stuffy nose, mild swelling at the contact site): monitor closely for worsening.
Anaphylaxis signs: swelling of face/tongue/throat, hives, trouble breathing, dizziness, or feeling faint - call 911 immediately.
If the person has their own epinephrine auto-injector, help them use it (or administer it if you're trained) right away - don't wait to see if it's 'bad enough.'
If symptoms haven't improved 5-10 minutes after the first dose and EMS hasn't arrived, a second dose may be given if available.
more_info: Antihistamines (like Benadryl) may ease minor symptoms but do NOT treat anaphylaxis and should never be used as a substitute for epinephrine.

title: Heat Exhaustion & Heat Stroke
summary: Heat stroke (hot, dry/red skin, confusion) is a 911 emergency - cool the person immediately.
quick_actions: Heat exhaustion: heavy sweating, cool/pale/clammy skin, dizziness, nausea - move to a cool place, sip water, loosen clothing, cool with a damp cloth.
Heat stroke: hot/red/dry skin, confusion, body temp over 103°F, possible unconsciousness - call 911 immediately.
While waiting for help with heat stroke, cool the person by any means available (cool water, wet cloths, fanning) - don't wait for symptoms to worsen further.
Get medical help for heat exhaustion too if symptoms last over an hour or get worse.
more_info: Heat stroke can be fatal without rapid cooling and medical care - it's a true emergency, not just "very tired from the heat."

title: Hypothermia & Frostbite
summary: Warm the person gradually - never with direct high heat, and never rub frostbitten skin.
quick_actions: Hypothermia signs: uncontrollable shivering, confusion, slurred speech, drowsiness - a body temp below 95°F is an emergency, call 911.
Move to a warm, dry place; remove wet clothing; warm the chest/neck/head/groin first with blankets or dry layers.
Frostbite signs: numbness, waxy or grayish-white skin - rewarm gradually in warm (not hot) water; do not rub or massage the area.
Do not give alcohol, and don't apply direct high heat (like a heating pad or fire) directly to skin - it can burn numb tissue without the person feeling it.
more_info: Severe hypothermia can slow breathing and pulse enough to seem absent - keep checking and don't assume the worst before EMS confirms.

title: Insect Bites, Stings & Snake Bites
summary: Watch for allergic reaction after any sting; call 911 immediately for any snake bite.
quick_actions: Insect sting: scrape out a visible stinger (don't squeeze it), wash with soap and water, apply a cold pack.
Watch closely for signs of allergic reaction/anaphylaxis for at least 30 minutes after any sting (see that topic).
Snake bite: call 911 immediately. Keep the person calm and still, and keep the bitten limb below heart level if possible.
Do NOT cut the wound, apply ice, use a tourniquet, or attempt suction on a snake bite - these can make things worse.
more_info: Don't waste time trying to catch or identify the snake - describing its appearance to EMS after the fact is enough, and delays care.

title: First-Aid Kit Reference
summary: A basic kit covers most minor injuries and buys time for anything bigger.
quick_actions: Wound care: adhesive bandages (assorted sizes), gauze pads and roller gauze, adhesive tape, antiseptic wipes, antibiotic ointment.
Tools: nonlatex gloves, tweezers, small scissors, an instant cold compress, a breathing barrier/CPR mask.
Medication: any personal prescriptions (epinephrine auto-injector, inhaler, etc.), pain reliever, hydrocortisone cream.
Other: emergency blanket, hand sanitizer - and check/replace expired items periodically.
more_info: Tailor contents to your household - known allergies, medications, and activities (vehicle, hiking, home) all change what's actually useful to include.
